title: Pore‐Scale Modeling of Fracture Evolution Driven by Dual‐Mineral Dissolution With Contrasting Reactivity and Morphology
content:
Abstract

Predictive models for reactive flow in fractured media often adopt single-mineral simplifications, neglecting feedback between mineralogical heterogeneity and hydrological evolution. This study investigates the pore-scale dynamics of fracture evolution in dual-mineral systems characterized by contrasting mineral reactivities and morphologies across varying Péclet and Damköhler numbers, using pore-scale reactive transport simulations. The results show that dual-mineral systems can accelerate total dissolution rates by suppressing local saturation buildup through ion-partitioned saturation control. However, this enhanced chemical reactivity does not necessarily result in permeability enhancement. Reactivity contrast sustains hydraulic resistance when the slower-reacting phase persists, limiting effective aperture widening even under fast bulk dissolution conditions. We identify a mineral-size-dependent permeability reversal phenomenon, where systems with smaller mineral clusters initially restrict flow due to dense clustering but eventually achieve higher permeability than large-cluster systems upon complete dissolution. An empirical phase diagram is developed to characterize armored, compact, and uniform dissolution regimes, and a sigmoid function is proposed to capture the asymptotic evolution of permeability. Mineral surface area evolution also deviates from conventional porous media models, exhibiting near-flat responses in the uniform regime due to a balance between mineral removal and newly exposed surface area. Finally, it is shown that conventional upscaled reaction rate relationships underestimate dissolution of the slow-reacting phase when its surface is newly exposed to undersaturated fluid. These findings highlight that predicting fracture alterations in subsurface environments requires accounting for the coupled effects of pore-scale mineral morphology, reactivity contrasts, and evolving porosity-permeability, surface area, and reaction rate relationships.
